title: Universal Suppression of Dissipation across Conformal Interface in Open Quantum Critical Systems
authors: Ruhanshi Barad, Tian Wu, Qicheng Tang, Xueda Wen
abstract: Conformal interfaces provide an important setting for studying universal transmission phenomena in one-dimensional quantum critical systems. While energy and information transmission across such interfaces are characterized by universal quantities in closed systems, the corresponding role of conformal interfaces in dissipative dynamics is less understood. In this work, we study relaxation in locally dissipative quantum critical chains with a conformal interface and show that a universal characterization emerges at the level of individual relaxation modes. We first show that the relaxation coefficient defined in the recent work [1] from the Liouvillian gap can become non-universal for certain boundary conditions because the mode determining the smallest decay rate can change as the interface transmission is varied. To resolve this ambiguity, we introduce a mode-resolved relaxation coefficient $c_{\rm relax}$ by continuously tracking the same Liouvillian rapidity mode as a function of the interface transmission. Using analytical and numerical calculations for a critical harmonic chain and a critical free-fermion chain, we find that, in the weak-dissipation regime, $c_{\rm relax}$ follows the same universal dependence on the interface transmission in all cases considered, independent of microscopic details such as the boundary conditions, dissipation strength, and location of the local dissipation. For boundary dissipation, this universal behavior persists even at finite dissipation strength. Our results establish a universal mode-resolved characterization of relaxation across conformal interfaces in open quantum critical systems.
summary: This work addresses how dissipation behaves across a conformal interface in quantum critical systems. The authors introduce a mode-resolved relaxation coefficient that successfully captures the universal physics, resolving ambiguities found in previous global measures. This establishes a robust, universal framework for characterizing dissipation in open quantum systems at critical points.
main_problem: The paper investigates the role of conformal interfaces in characterizing dissipation and relaxation dynamics within open quantum critical systems.
main_result: A newly defined mode-resolved relaxation coefficient ($c_{	ext{relax}}$) was shown to be universal, maintaining a consistent dependence on interface transmission regardless of microscopic details or boundary conditions.
method: The authors employed analytical and numerical calculations on critical harmonic and free-fermion chains, focusing on tracking individual relaxation modes rather than relying solely on the global Liouvillian gap.
model_or_system: The study models locally dissipative quantum critical chains connected by a conformal interface, analyzed using techniques derived from Lindblad master equations and non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonians.
key_observables: Mode-resolved relaxation coefficient ($c_{	ext{relax}}$), global relaxation coefficient ($c_{	ext{global}}^{	ext{relax}}$), energy/information transmission coefficients ($c_{	ext{LR}}, c_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Interface transmission coefficient ($t$), dissipation strength ($\gamma$), and the weak-dissipation regime.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the applicability of mode-resolved tracking to resolve ambiguities found in global gap measurements.
figures_summary: Figures compare the non-universal behavior of the global relaxation coefficient against the universal behavior of the mode-resolved coefficient as a function of interface transmission.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of non-universality in global relaxation measures, then introduces the mode-resolved coefficient, and finally validates its universal behavior using specific critical chain models.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, universal characterization of dissipation suppression across quantum interfaces, which is crucial for understanding non-equilibrium steady states in critical systems relevant to quantum optics and condensed matter.
